title: Retention policies per folder
description:
Tenants that store logs, exports or scratch files want them gone after a while without running their own delete scripts. This adds retention rules per folder, applied by the cleanup job.

- Migration 0004: `retention_rules(tenant_id, prefix, days)`, one rule per tenant and prefix; the prefix is a folder ending with `/`, days from 1 to 36500.
- `PUT /v1/retention/<folder>/` with `{"days"}` creates or changes a rule, `DELETE /v1/retention/<folder>/` removes it (both `tenant:admin`), `GET /v1/retention` lists them (`tenant:read`). Prefixes are validated with the new `normalizeFolderPrefix` (a valid path plus `/`). A tenant has at most 100 rules; `RetentionService.setRule` locks the tenant row while counting so concurrent requests cannot pass the limit.
- When several of a tenant's rules match a path, the one with the longest prefix applies (`logs/` at 30 days, `logs/audit/` at 3650 days). Days count as 24 hours regardless of the database session's time zone.
- New cleanup step `applyRetention`, between session expiry and the purge step: `retentionRepo.findExpiredFiles` picks up to `CLEANUP_BATCH_SIZE` live files whose rule says they are due, oldest first; each one is marked deleted and its bytes released in a transaction of its own (no long transaction across a whole batch), then its object is removed. `retentionRepo.expireFile` reads the rule again in its UPDATE, so a file whose rule was removed or lengthened after the batch was picked stays. An object that cannot be removed is left to `purgeDeletedObjects`. `CleanupReport` gains `expiredFiles`.
- README: Retention paragraph, API table and rule format.

Tests in `test/api/retention.test.ts`: rule CRUD and tenant isolation, validation, scopes and the rule limit, the age boundary with released bytes and removed objects, longest-prefix precedence, files of every live status in several batches, other tenants untouched, and rules removed or lengthened while the job is running.

bugs.summary: applyRetention selects the due files without any lock, then for each one runs retentionRepo.expireFile, whose UPDATE matches the row by id alone (no `AND status <> 'deleted'`, row count ignored), and calls releaseBytes(file.size) unconditionally. When the file is deleted by someone else between the SELECT and the UPDATE - a user's DELETE /v1/files/<path>, an overwrite (FileCatalog.register), or a second instance running the same cleanup step - the UPDATE waits for that transaction, then marks the already-deleted row again and the job releases its bytes a second time. used_bytes drops below the bytes the tenant actually stores, so the quota no longer holds (the tenant can upload that much extra), and the object is removed twice and deleted_at rewritten. Because the row count is ignored, the same happens when expireFile's own rule re-check matches nothing (the rule was removed or lengthened after the SELECT): the file stays live but its bytes are released and its object removed.
bugs.trigger: Rule old/ 30 days, files old/a (100 B), old/b (200 B), keep/c (1000 B), clock 31 days later. A user's delete of old/a is in progress (row marked deleted, 100 B released, not yet committed) when the cleanup job selects; it commits while the job waits on the row: used_bytes ends at 900 instead of 1000. Two cleanup runs that pick the same files end at 700.
bugs.false_rebuttal: A double release cannot hurt the books: tenantRepo.releaseBytes updates used_bytes with GREATEST(used_bytes - $2, 0) and logs when it releases more than is used, so a second release of an already-released file is clamped and reported rather than corrupting the tenant's usage.
